CHAPTER 2 · LEARNING AREA 2

CHAPTER 2 · LEARNING AREA 2 · DECEMBER

Circle, cylinder and sphere

A slice of pizza, a tin can, a steel ball: wherever something is round, the number $\pi$ is in it. You calculate arcs and sectors, the surface area and volume of cylinders and spheres and, with the density, also their mass. And you find out which result Archimedes was so proud of that he had it put on his gravestone.

8 LESSONS2 UNITS3 LABS
WHAT YOU WILL LEARN IN THIS CHAPTER
  • calculate the circumference and area of circles confidently
  • calculate arcs, sectors and annuli and split up composite areas
  • find the surface area and volume of cylinders and spheres
  • calculate the mass of a solid from its density
CHECK-IN: CAN YOU ALREADY DO THIS?

A circle has a radius of 5 cm. How large is its diameter?

$d = 2r = 10$ cm

How do you calculate the area of a circle?

$2\pi r$ is the circumference.

How many cubic centimetres are there in a litre?

$1\,\ell = 1\,\text{dm}^3 = 1000\,\text{cm}^3$

A prism has a base area of 12 cm² and a height of 5 cm. Volume?

$V = G \cdot h = 60$ cm³

EXPLORATIONSTO GET STARTED · IN GROUPS
THE BIGGEST SLICE

A pizza 30 cm across is cut into 8 equal slices, one 26 cm across into 6.

  • For which pizza is a slice bigger? How long is the crust of one slice?
  • How are the crust, the area and the angle of a slice related to the whole circle?

  • Calculate how much fits inside and compare with what is printed on the tin.

CAVALIERI’S PRINCIPLEEqual cross-sections, equal volume
UNIT 14 LESSONS

1Circle and parts of a circle

An eighth of the 30 cm pizza is a sector with $r = 15$ cm and $\alpha = 45^\circ$. Its area is an eighth of the area of the circle: $\tfrac18 \cdot \pi \cdot 15^2 \approx 88$ cm². A sixth of the 26 cm pizza has $\tfrac16 \cdot \pi \cdot 13^2 \approx 88.5$ cm². Almost the same; the sixth wins narrowly.

A sector with the angle at the centre $\alpha$ is the fraction $\tfrac{\alpha}{360^\circ}$ of the circle. Its edge on the circle is called an arc. An annulus (ring) lies between two circles with a common centre.

KEY POINT · CIRCLE AND PARTS OF A CIRCLE

Circle: circumference $u = 2\pi r = \pi d$ · area $A = \pi r^2$ · $\pi \approx 3.14159$

Arc: $b = \dfrac{\alpha}{360^\circ} \cdot 2\pi r$ · sector: $A = \dfrac{\alpha}{360^\circ} \cdot \pi r^2 = \tfrac12\,b\,r$

Annulus with the radii $r_a > r_i$: $A = \pi\left(r_a^2 - r_i^2\right)$

Memory aid: $A = \tfrac12\,b\,r$ looks like the triangle formula. A narrow sector is almost a triangle with base $b$ and height $r$.

Rounding: calculate with the $\pi$ key and only round at the end. $3.14$ is too inaccurate for many purposes.

INTERACTIVE · ARC AND SECTOR

Drag the end of the arc or use the sliders. The fraction of the full circle is in both formulas.

EXAMPLE 1 · A SLICE OF PIZZA

Calculate the length of the crust and the area of an eighth of a pizza 30 cm across.

$b = \tfrac18 \cdot 2\pi \cdot 15 \approx 11.78$ cm, $A = \tfrac18 \cdot \pi \cdot 15^2 \approx 88.36$ cm².

Crust 11.8 cm, area 88.4 cm²

EXAMPLE 2 · COMPOSITE

A window consists of a rectangle 1 m wide and 1.20 m high with a semicircle on top. Calculate the area of glass and the length of the frame.

$A = 1 \cdot 1.2 + \tfrac12 \pi \cdot 0.5^2 \approx 1.2 + 0.39 = 1.59$ m².

Frame: $1 + 2 \cdot 1.2 + \tfrac12 \cdot \pi \cdot 1 \approx 4.97$ m. 1.59 m² of glass, 4.97 m of frame

EXERCISES

Calculate the circumference and the area: a) $r = 4$ cm   b) $d = 10$ m   c) $r = 0.5$ mm

a) $25.13$ cm; $50.27$ cm²   b) $31.42$ m; $78.54$ m²   c) $3.14$ mm; $0.79$ mm²

Calculate the arc length and the area of the sector: a) $r = 6$ cm, $\alpha = 120^\circ$   b) $r = 10$ cm, $\alpha = 90^\circ$   c) $r = 3$ m, $\alpha = 300^\circ$

a) $12.57$ cm; $37.70$ cm²   b) $15.71$ cm; $78.54$ cm²   c) $15.71$ m; $23.56$ m²

The minute hand of a clock is 12 cm long. How far does its tip travel in 20 minutes, and what area does it sweep over?

20 minutes are $\tfrac13$ of a turn: $b = \tfrac13 \cdot 2\pi \cdot 12 \approx 25.13$ cm, $A = \tfrac13 \cdot \pi \cdot 144 \approx 150.80$ cm².

A washer has an outer diameter of 24 mm and an inner diameter of 13 mm. What is its area?

$A = \pi\left(12^2 - 6.5^2\right) = \pi \cdot 101.75 \approx 319.66$ mm²

A sector with $r = 5$ cm has an area of 20 cm². How long is its arc, and how large is its angle at the centre?

$A = \tfrac12 b r \Rightarrow b = \tfrac{2 \cdot 20}{5} = 8$ cm. $\alpha = \tfrac{20}{25\pi} \cdot 360^\circ \approx 91.7^\circ$.

TEST YOURSELF!

What is the circumference of a circle with $r = 5$ cm?

$10\pi \approx 31.42$ cm

What is the area of a semicircle with $r = 2$ cm?

$\tfrac12 \pi \cdot 4 = 2\pi \approx 6.28$ cm²

What is the area of a sector with $r = 6$ cm and $\alpha = 60^\circ$?

$\tfrac16 \pi \cdot 36 = 6\pi \approx 18.85$ cm²

UNIT 24 LESSONS

2Cylinder and sphere

A cylinder is a prism with a circle as its base. That is why, as for the prism, $V = G \cdot h$. If you unroll its curved surface, you get a rectangle: as high as the cylinder and as wide as the circumference of the base circle.

For the sphere there is no curved surface to unroll. Archimedes found its formulas by comparing it with a cylinder. With the density $\varrho$ of a material, the mass per volume, you get the mass from the volume.

KEY POINT · CYLINDER, SPHERE, MASS

Cylinder (radius $r$, height $h$): $V = \pi r^2 h$ · curved surface $M = 2\pi r h$ · surface area $O = 2\pi r^2 + 2\pi r h$

Sphere (radius $r$): $V = \tfrac43 \pi r^3$ · surface area $O = 4\pi r^2$

Mass: $m = \varrho \cdot V$. Water has $\varrho = 1\,\tfrac{\text{g}}{\text{cm}^3}$, steel about $7.85\,\tfrac{\text{g}}{\text{cm}^3}$, gold $19.3\,\tfrac{\text{g}}{\text{cm}^3}$.

Units: lengths in cm give areas in cm² and volumes in cm³. $1\,\text{cm}^3 = 1\,\text{m}\ell$, $1\,\text{dm}^3 = 1\,\ell$.

Powers: double the radius gives four times the surface area and eight times the volume. You know that from chapter 1.2.

INTERACTIVE · ROUND SOLIDS

Set the radius and the height. You only need the cone in chapter 3.3; it is already here for comparison.

EXAMPLE 3 · A TIN

A tin can is 10 cm across and 12 cm high. How much fits inside, and how much sheet metal do you need?

$V = \pi \cdot 5^2 \cdot 12 \approx 942.5$ cm³, so just under a litre.

$O = 2\pi \cdot 25 + 2\pi \cdot 5 \cdot 12 \approx 157.1 + 377.0$: $O \approx 534.1$ cm²

EXAMPLE 4 · A STEEL BALL

How heavy is a steel ball 4 cm across ($\varrho = 7.85\,\tfrac{\text{g}}{\text{cm}^3}$)?

$V = \tfrac43 \pi \cdot 2^3 \approx 33.51$ cm³.

$m = 7.85 \cdot 33.51 \approx$ 263 g

EXERCISES

Calculate the volume and the surface area of a cylinder with $r = 5$ cm and $h = 8$ cm.

$V = 200\pi \approx 628.32$ cm³ · $O = 50\pi + 80\pi = 130\pi \approx 408.41$ cm²

Calculate the volume and the surface area of a sphere with $r = 6$ cm. How large is the surface area of the Earth (radius about 6370 km)?

$V = 288\pi \approx 904.78$ cm³, $O = 144\pi \approx 452.39$ cm². Earth: $4\pi \cdot 6370^2 \approx 5.1 \cdot 10^8$ km².

A cylindrical tin is to be 10 cm high and hold exactly one litre. What radius does it need?

$\pi r^2 \cdot 10 = 1000 \Rightarrow r = \sqrt{\tfrac{100}{\pi}} \approx 5.64$ cm

One kilogram of gold ($\varrho = 19.3\,\tfrac{\text{g}}{\text{cm}^3}$) is cast into a sphere. What is its diameter?

$V = \tfrac{1000}{19.3} \approx 51.81$ cm³, $r = \sqrt[3]{\tfrac{3V}{4\pi}} \approx 2.31$ cm: diameter about 4.6 cm.

A sphere fits exactly into a cylinder ($h = 2r$). Show that its volume is two thirds of the volume of the cylinder, and that the same holds for the surface areas.

$V_Z = \pi r^2 \cdot 2r = 2\pi r^3$, $V_K = \tfrac43 \pi r^3 = \tfrac23 V_Z$. $O_Z = 2\pi r^2 + 2\pi r \cdot 2r = 6\pi r^2$, $O_K = 4\pi r^2 = \tfrac23 O_Z$.

TEST YOURSELF!

Volume of a cylinder with $r = 2$ cm and $h = 5$ cm?

$20\pi \approx 62.83$ cm³

Surface area of a sphere with $r = 1$ cm?

$4\pi \approx 12.57$ cm²

What fraction of the circumscribed cylinder does a sphere fill?

$\tfrac23$

REVIEW · DEEPEN · CONNECT

A lawn sprinkler reaches 8 m and turns through 270°. How much lawn does it water?

$\tfrac34 \cdot \pi \cdot 64 \approx 150.8$ m²

Three tennis balls (diameter 6.7 cm) are in a cylindrical tin that is exactly as wide and three times as high. What fraction of the tin is air?

The tin consists of three cylinders with one ball each, and each ball fills $\tfrac23$. So $\tfrac13$, about 33%, is air, whatever the size.

Connecting with chapter 1.1: what radius does a sphere have that holds exactly one litre? How does its volume change if the radius grows by 10%?

$r = \sqrt[3]{\tfrac{3000}{4\pi}} \approx 6.20$ cm. $1.1^3 = 1.331$: the volume grows by a good 33%.

A rope lies tight around the equator. It is made 1 m longer and lifted to the same height everywhere. Will a cat fit underneath? And would it be different for a rope round a football?

$2\pi(r + x) = 2\pi r + 1 \Rightarrow x = \tfrac{1}{2\pi} \approx 0.16$ m. A cat almost fits underneath. The result does not depend on the radius: for the football it is 16 cm as well.

EXCURSIONHISTORY

The tomb of Archimedes

Archimedes of Syracuse (around 287 to 212 BC) proved in his work “On the Sphere and Cylinder” that a sphere fills exactly two thirds of the cylinder it fits into, and that its surface area is also two thirds of the cylinder’s surface area. The surface of the sphere is even exactly as large as the curved surface of the cylinder.

He considered this result his finest. He wished for a sphere inside a cylinder on his tomb. About 140 years after his death the Roman politician Cicero searched for the forgotten tomb in Syracuse. He found it, overgrown with thorns, by exactly this picture and a half-weathered inscription.

Sources: Archimedes, On the Sphere and Cylinder I, proposition 34 with corollary. Marcus Tullius Cicero, Tusculanae disputationes V, 64–66.

$\tfrac14 \cdot 4\pi = \pi$

A cylinder has $r = 3$ and $h = 4$. Its volume is $k \cdot \pi$. What is $k$?

$9 \cdot 4 = 36$

A sphere has $r = 3$. Its surface area is $k \cdot \pi$. What is $k$?

$4 \cdot 9 = 36$

$\pi(144 - 42.25)$

What radius does a one-litre tin 10 cm high need?

$\sqrt{100/\pi}$

Mass of a steel ball with $d = 4$ cm, $\varrho = 7.85\,\text{g/cm}^3$?
